arml-local-2013-theme-01.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) A knight moves either two squares horizontally and one square vertically, or two squares vertically and one square horizontally, and it can jump over other pieces. Compute the minimum number of moves to exchange the positions of the two white and black knights on the $3\times3$ board as shown in the graphic (white knights in the top corners and black knights in the bottom corners at the start; after the exchange the colours are swapped). Two knights may not occupy the same square at the same time. Alternating black and white knight moves is not required.

arml-local-2013-theme-02.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) A knight moves either two squares horizontally and one square vertically, or two squares vertically and one square horizontally, and it can jump over other pieces. Compute the minimum number of moves to change the position on the left of the graphic (on a board of $13$ squares) into the position on the right, in which the two white and black knights have exchanged their squares. Two knights may not occupy the same square at the same time. Alternating black and white knight moves is not required.

arml-local-2013-theme-03.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) A *hexaknight* moves either two squares horizontally, or two squares vertically and one square horizontally (six possible moves). On the $3\times10$ board shown, the grey squares are squares of the other colour that the hexaknight cannot use, so only the white squares matter; the hexaknight starts in the upper left corner and wants to reach the lower right corner. Two of the eight non-corner white squares are now also coloured gray. If all eight squares are equally likely to be the ones coloured gray, compute the probability (as a fraction) that there exists a path for the hexaknight in the upper left corner to reach the lower right corner of the board while travelling only on white squares.

arml-local-2013-theme-04.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) A *hexaknight* moves either two squares horizontally, or two squares vertically and one square horizontally (six possible moves). On the $3\times10$ board shown, the grey squares are squares of the other colour that the hexaknight cannot use, so only the white squares matter; the hexaknight starts in the upper left corner and wants to reach the lower right corner. Three of the eight non-corner white squares are now also coloured gray. If all eight squares are equally likely to be the ones coloured gray, compute the probability (as a fraction) that there exists a path for the hexaknight in the upper left corner to reach the lower right corner of the board while travelling only on white squares.

arml-local-2013-theme-05.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) A knight moves either two squares horizontally and one square vertically, or two squares vertically and one square horizontally, and it can jump over other pieces. Consider the path formed by joining in order the centres of the squares visited by a knight. The path is *simple* if none of the edges cross in their interiors and is *closed* if the knight returns to the square where it began. (In the example board shown, the white knight's path is simple but not closed, while the black knight's path is closed but not simple.) If the centres of adjacent squares are one unit apart, compute the maximum area enclosed by a knight's simple closed path on an $8\times8$ board.

arml-local-2013-theme-06.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) A knight moves either two squares horizontally and one square vertically, or two squares vertically and one square horizontally, and it can jump over other pieces. On a board, a square is considered *attacked* if it contains a knight or can be reached by a knight in one move (on the $5\times5$ board with a knight in the centre, nine squares are attacked). Two knights are randomly placed on distinct squares of a $3\times3$ board, with all squares equally likely. Compute the expected number of squares that are attacked.

arml-local-2013-theme-07.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) A knight moves either two squares horizontally and one square vertically, or two squares vertically and one square horizontally, and it can jump over other pieces. A square is *attacked* if it contains a knight or can be reached by a knight in one move. Compute the minimum number of knights needed to attack every square of a $4\times6$ board.

arml-local-2013-theme-08.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) A knight moves either two squares horizontally and one square vertically, or two squares vertically and one square horizontally, and it can jump over other pieces. **Estimation problem** (in the contest, an answer within $10\%$ of the correct value earned credit). A knight is on a square on an infinite chessboard. Compute the number of distinct squares where the knight can end up after exactly $10$ moves.
arml-local-2013-theme-08.answer: $741$ (any estimate from $666.9$ to $815.1$ was accepted in the contest)

arml-local-2013-theme-09.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) For integers $m$ and $n$ with $0\le m\le n$, an $(m,n)$-restricted knight can only move either up $m$ squares and right $n$ squares, or up $n$ squares and right $m$ squares. The possible moves of a $(1,2)$-restricted knight are shown in the figure. Compute the number of distinct paths a $(1,2)$-restricted knight can take from the lower left corner to the upper right corner of a $10\times10$ board.

arml-local-2013-theme-10.prompt: (Theme: knights on a chessboard.) For integers $m$ and $n$ with $0\le m\le n$, an $(m,n)$-restricted knight can only move either up $m$ squares and right $n$ squares, or up $n$ squares and right $m$ squares. Compute the number of ordered pairs $(m,n)$ with $0\le m\le n$ such that there exist at least $20$ distinct paths for an $(m,n)$-restricted knight from the lower left corner to the upper right corner of a $17\times17$ board.
